description: Liturgical and non-liturgical worship, sacraments across denominations, and the nature of prayer.
content_html:
Forms of Christian Worship

Worship is how Christians express love and devotion to God. Christians worship in several distinct forms, and different denominations emphasise different approaches. This spec point is starred (2.1*), meaning students must compare Christian worship with that of another religion in the exam.

Liturgical worship follows a fixed, formal structure. Anglican services follow the Book of Common Prayer (or its modern successor, Common Worship); Catholic services follow the Roman Rite; Orthodox services follow centuries-old liturgical patterns. The advantage is that worshippers know what to expect, the service connects them to centuries of Christian tradition, and the same words unite Christians globally. Anglicans, Catholics and Orthodox all use liturgical worship as their primary form.

Non-liturgical worship is less structured and more flexible. It is common in Methodist, Baptist and many Reformed churches. There is no prescribed prayer book; sermons are central; hymns and readings are chosen to suit the congregation’s needs. Some Christians prefer this form because it allows the Spirit to guide the service rather than following a predetermined script.

Key Fact

The Book of Common Prayer (1662 version) is the historical service book of the Church of England, providing set liturgies for Morning Prayer, Evening Prayer, Holy Communion and other rites. It shaped Anglican worship for centuries and remains in use today, especially in traditional parish churches. Many Anglicans also use the modern Common Worship (2000) book. The Book of Common Prayer is a specific Edexcel-named source — knowing its name and denominational context is essential for 5-mark source questions.

Pentecostal churches (and charismatic congregations in other denominations) worship very differently from liturgical traditions. Services are spontaneous and led by the Spirit: worship includes contemporary music with guitars, drums and clapping; congregants may speak in tongues (glossolalia), give prophecies, pray aloud spontaneously and respond physically. There is no fixed order of service and no prayer book. Pentecostal worship has grown rapidly in the UK and globally — it is the fastest-growing Christian expression worldwide. The contrast between Pentecostal and Anglican/Catholic liturgical worship is a prime example for exam questions on denominational diversity.

This spec point is starred (2.1*) â€” students must compare Christian worship with another tradition. The most common exam comparison is with Islam. Similarities: Both Christian and Islamic worship include communal prayer, reading from sacred scripture, and acts of praise directed towards God. Friday Jumu'ah prayers in Islam and Sunday services in Christianity both serve as the primary communal worship event of the week. Differences: Islamic Salah is highly ritualised (five set times daily, specific bodily postures, Arabic recitation, ritual purity required); Christian worship varies enormously from the Pentecostal free-flowing to the Catholic Mass. Islamic worship is strictly non-sacramental; Christian worship often centres on sacramental acts (Eucharist, baptism). Islam explicitly rejects the use of music and images in worship in many traditions; Christianity has a rich tradition of sacred music and art.

Sacraments in Different Denominations

A sacrament is an outward, visible sign of an inward, spiritual reality. The number of sacraments is a significant denominational difference. Catholic and Orthodox Christians recognise seven sacraments: Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Penance (Reconciliation), Anointing of the Sick, Holy Orders and Matrimony. Most Protestant churches recognise only two — Baptism and the Eucharist (Lord’s Supper) — because only these two were explicitly commanded by Jesus in the Gospels. The 39 Articles XXV–XXXVI are the Anglican doctrinal statement on sacraments: Article XXV affirms two sacraments “ordained of Christ our Lord in the Gospel” (Baptism and the Supper of the Lord) and describes the five other Catholic sacraments as “not to be counted for Sacraments of the Gospel.”

Baptism is the sacrament of initiation into the Christian community — widely practised across denominations. The mode and timing vary: Catholics, Anglicans and Orthodox baptise infants (paedo-baptism); Baptists and many evangelicals baptise only those who have made a personal declaration of faith (believer’s baptism). The meaning also varies: in Catholic and Orthodox theology, baptism washes away original sin and incorporates the person into the Body of Christ; in Protestant theology, it is primarily a sign of inclusion in the covenant community and a declaration of faith.

The Eucharist (also called Holy Communion, the Lord’s Supper or the Mass) is the other universally accepted sacrament. However, what happens during the Eucharist is one of Christianity’s most significant theological disputes. Catholics teach transubstantiation: the substance of the bread and wine is truly transformed into the body and blood of Christ, though the outward appearance remains. Most Protestants either hold a memorialist view (bread and wine are symbols only, recalling Christ’s sacrifice) or a spiritual presence view (Christ is genuinely but spiritually present in the sharing). The Anglican Thirty-Nine Articles deliberately leave room for both views.

Prayer: Set and Informal

Prayer is a central Christian practice. Jesus taught about prayer in Matthew 6:5–14: he warned against ostentatious public praying done to impress others, and instructed his followers to pray in private and to use a model he gave them — the Lord’s Prayer. Christians use two main types of prayer. Set prayers are written texts used repeatedly — for example, the Lord’s Prayer, the General Confession from the Book of Common Prayer, or prayers from liturgical books. They provide unity, connect worshippers to tradition, and are especially central in liturgical worship. Informal prayer uses the believer’s own words, allowing personal and spontaneous expression of faith.

Key Fact

The Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:9–13) is the model prayer Jesus gave his disciples. It is the one prayer shared by virtually all Christian denominations worldwide, said in liturgical services, at weddings, baptisms and funerals. Its structure includes: address to God as Father in heaven; hallowing of his name (praise); petition for God’s kingdom to come; request for daily bread (provision); request for forgiveness; and protection from temptation and evil. It teaches Christians that prayer should combine praise, submission to God’s will, requests for daily needs and forgiveness.
exam_tip_html: Worship (2.1*) is a starred comparison point — in a 12-mark Discuss question you may be asked to compare Christian worship with that of another religion. Always develop both sides: “Christians … [named denomination + source]; in contrast, Muslims ….” For a 5-mark source question on prayer, the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:5–14) and the Book of Common Prayer are both named Edexcel sources — either earns the 5th mark if properly attributed and developed. The most common student error on sacraments questions is stating only that “Catholics have seven and Protestants have two” without developing why Protestants reduced the number (only baptism and Eucharist were commanded by Jesus in the Gospels) or what the 39 Articles say specifically. SPaG marks: ‘Eucharist’, ‘liturgical’, ‘sacrament’ and ‘Pentecostal’ are high-value specialist terms — spell them correctly.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Christian worship ranges from liturgical (fixed structure, Book of Common Prayer, Catholic Mass) to non-liturgical (flexible, Bible-centred) to Pentecostal (spontaneous, Spirit-led) — this spec point is starred (2.1*) requiring comparison with another religion such as Islam.
  • Most Protestant churches recognise two sacraments (Baptism and Eucharist, as commanded by Jesus â€” 39 Articles XXV); Catholics and Orthodox recognise seven; key Eucharist difference: Catholics teach transubstantiation, most Protestants hold a memorialist or spiritual-presence view.
  • Prayer includes set prayers (e.g. the Lord's Prayer, Matthew 6:9-13) and informal prayer; Jesus taught that prayer should combine praise, submission, request and forgiveness, and warned against ostentatious displays (Matthew 6:5).

practice_questions.text: Outline three features of liturgical Christian worship.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each of three discrete, accurate points. Acceptable points include:
- Liturgical worship follows a fixed, formal structure (set prayers, set responses).
- It is used by Anglican, Catholic and Orthodox Christians.
- The Book of Common Prayer (Anglican) or Roman Rite (Catholic) provides the set texts.
- A minister or priest leads the congregation through the set order.
- The Eucharist/Mass is typically central to liturgical worship.
Do not award marks for three sentences that elaborate the same point.

practice_questions.text: Describe how Pentecostal Christians worship differently from Anglican Christians.
practice_questions.marks:
Acceptable content:
- Pentecostal worship is spontaneous and led by the Holy Spirit; there is no fixed order of service or prayer book.
- It may include speaking in tongues (glossolalia), prophecy, healing prayer and contemporary music with guitars and clapping.
- Anglican worship is liturgical â€” following the set structure of the Book of Common Prayer or Common Worship, with set prayers and responses led by a minister.
[1 mark per accurate contrasting point, up to 3]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Christian beliefs about sacraments differ between denominations.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- Catholics and Orthodox Christians recognise seven sacraments; most Protestant traditions (including Anglicans, as stated in the 39 Articles XXV) recognise only two â€” baptism and the Eucharist. Protestants reduced the number because only these two were explicitly commanded by Jesus in the Gospels; the five Catholic sacraments are described in the 39 Articles as not being 'Sacraments of the Gospel.'
- The meaning of the Eucharist differs significantly: Catholics teach transubstantiation â€” the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ (the outward appearance remains but the substance changes). Most Protestant Christians hold either a memorialist view (bread and wine are symbols only) or a spiritual presence view (Christ is spiritually but not physically present). This is one of the most significant points of division in the Reformation.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Christians use set prayers, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.type: 5 marks â€” Explain Two with Sources
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations (2 marks each) plus a named source (1 mark).

Acceptable explanations:
- Set prayers connect Christians to centuries of tradition and unite believers across denominations: the Lord's Prayer is said in virtually all Christian services worldwide, from Catholic Mass to Baptist Sunday worship. Matthew 6:9-13 records Jesus specifically teaching this prayer to his disciples as a model â€” its regular use keeps Christians grounded in the pattern Jesus himself gave.
- Set prayers provide a reliable structure for worship, especially for those who struggle to find words: the Book of Common Prayer gives worshippers tested, beautiful language for confession, thanksgiving and praise. Using the same words as Christians across generations creates a sense of continuity with the historic Church.

The 5th mark: name a specific source â€” 'Matthew 6:9-13 (the Lord's Prayer)', 'the Book of Common Prayer' or another clearly identified text. Paraphrase without attribution does not earn the 5th mark.

practice_questions.text:
'Liturgical worship is more important than informal worship for Christians today.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion.

Secure (7-9): Both sides present; at least one named source; conclusion present.

Developing (4-6): One side more developed; limited sources; conclusion descriptive.

Emerging (1-3): One-sided; minimal development; no named sources.

Arguments in support:
- Liturgical worship connects Christians to centuries of tradition and provides a shared structure that unites the Church globally: the same Eucharistic prayers, the same Lord's Prayer, the same lectionary readings unite Catholics, Anglicans and Orthodox across the world. The Book of Common Prayer has shaped English-speaking Christianity for over 350 years.
- Liturgical worship is ordered and biblical: set scripture readings, the Nicene Creed and the Lord's Prayer ensure that core doctrine and key texts are rehearsed regularly. This guards against theological drift and ensures worshippers are formed by the whole of Scripture, not just a preacher's preferences.
- Sacraments (central to liturgical worship) are considered by Catholic, Orthodox and many Anglican Christians to be genuine channels of God's grace â€” not symbolic but effective. Without sacramental worship, Christians may miss out on the grace God intends to give through these means.

Arguments against:
- Pentecostal and charismatic worship has grown fastest globally, suggesting that many Christians find less structured, Spirit-led worship more meaningful and life-giving. Jesus himself warned against empty, repetitive prayer (Matthew 6:7 â€” 'do not keep on babbling'); liturgical services can become mechanical.
- Informal prayer allows Christians to bring their personal concerns before God in their own words: Jesus encouraged private, personal prayer in Matthew 6:6 ('go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father, who is unseen'). Formal liturgy cannot always meet the individual's specific spiritual needs.
- Many Baptist, Methodist and evangelical Christians argue that the New Testament church was not liturgical in the Catholic sense: the emphasis in the early Church was on preaching, communal prayer and breaking of bread in simple settings, not an elaborate ritual structure.

SPaG: 'liturgical', 'Eucharist', 'sacrament', 'Pentecostal' must be spelt correctly.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between Protestant and Catholic approaches to baptism.
practice_questions.marks:
Two developed explanations required.

Acceptable explanations:
- The timing of baptism differs: Catholics (and Anglicans, Orthodox) practise infant baptism (paedo-baptism), baptising babies into the community of faith, believing it removes original sin and incorporates the child into the Body of Christ. Baptists and many evangelicals practise believer's baptism â€” only those who have personally declared faith in Jesus are baptised, because it is seen as a public expression of individual faith.
- The theological meaning differs: in Catholic theology, baptism is a sacrament that confers grace, washes away original sin and makes the person a member of the Church. In Baptist theology, baptism is an ordinance â€” an act of obedience that publicly expresses a faith already present in the believer's heart. Grace is received through faith, not through the water of baptism.
[2 marks per explanation: 1 for point, 1 for development]

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following CORRECTLY describes the difference between Catholic and Protestant views on the number of sacraments?
options: Catholics recognise two sacraments; Protestants recognise seven
Catholics recognise seven sacraments; most Protestants recognise two (baptism and Eucharist)
Both traditions recognise exactly five sacraments
Catholics recognise ten sacraments; Protestants recognise none

knowledge_checks.q: The Book of Common Prayer is the historic service book of which denomination?
Pentecostal worship is characterised by spontaneous, Spirit-led services that may include speaking in _____ (glossolalia).
The Catholic teaching that the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ during the Eucharist is called _____.
Match each type of worship or prayer to its description:
right: Follows a fixed structure with set texts â€” e.g. the Book of Common Prayer or Roman Rite
Flexible service with no prescribed order, common in Baptist and Methodist churches
Prayer in the believer's own words, expressing personal concerns spontaneously

flashcard_questions.a: A church service following a fixed, formal structure with set prayers and responses.

flashcard_questions.q: The Book of Common Prayer is associated with which denomination?
How many sacraments do most Protestant churches recognise, and which two are they?
flashcard_questions.a: Two â€” baptism and the Eucharist (Lord's Supper), commanded by Jesus in the Gospels.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation teach about the Eucharist?
flashcard_questions.a: That the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the memorialist view of the Eucharist?
flashcard_questions.a: That the bread and wine are symbolic only â€” recalling Christ's sacrifice, not containing him.

flashcard_questions.q: Which articles of the 39 Articles deal with sacraments, and what do they say?
flashcard_questions.a: Articles XXV-XXXVI â€” affirming two Gospel sacraments (baptism and Eucharist); rejecting the other five as 'not Sacraments of the Gospel'.

flashcard_questions.q: Where in Matthew does Jesus teach the Lord's Prayer?
What is Pentecostal worship characterised by?
flashcard_questions.a: Spontaneous, Spirit-led services including speaking in tongues, contemporary music and healing prayer.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main difference between set prayers and informal prayer?
flashcard_questions.a: Set prayers are written texts used repeatedly (e.g. Lord's Prayer); informal prayer uses the believer's own words.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Jesus warn against in Matthew 6:5-7 regarding prayer?
flashcard_questions.a: Ostentatious public praying to impress others, and meaningless repetition.

flashcard_questions.q: What form of baptism do Baptist churches practise, and why?
flashcard_questions.a: Believer's baptism — adults are fully immersed after personally professing faith in Christ.

glossary_terms.definition: Acts of praise, honour and devotion directed towards God, either collectively or individually.
A church service that follows a set, formal structure with prescribed prayers and responses, often using a service book.
A church service without a fixed, written order â€” the minister has flexibility in how the service is structured.
A charismatic Christian denomination emphasising the direct experience of the Holy Spirit through speaking in tongues, healing, prophecy and spontaneous worship.
A sacred ritual through which Christians believe they receive God's grace; an outward, visible sign of an inward, spiritual blessing.
Also called Holy Communion or the Lord's Supper â€” the sacrament commemorating the Last Supper, in which bread and wine are shared.
Communication with God â€” Christians pray to praise God, confess sin, give thanks, ask for help and seek guidance.
